A_target.statement:
Let $g: \Bbb D^n \to \Bbb D^n$ be a [[Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)|continuous mapping]], where $\Bbb D^n$ is the [[Definition:Closed Unit Ball|closed unit ball]] of $\R^n$.
Then there exists $x \in \Bbb D^n$ such that:
:$\map g x = x$

B_source.statement:
There is no [[Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)|continuous mapping]] $r: \Bbb D^n \to \Bbb S^{n - 1}$ such that:
:$\forall x \in \Bbb S^{n - 1}: \map r x = x$
That is, $\Bbb S^{n - 1}$ is not a [[Definition:Retract (Topology)|retract]] of $\Bbb D^n$.

substitutions.a hypothetical fixed-point-free map g: the retraction r(x) = the boundary point on the ray from g(x) through x
substitutions.the ray from g(x) through x: the construction sending each x to a boundary point

derived.no such r exists: no fixed-point-free g exists, i.e. g has a fixed point

object_map.reformulation: Assume g has no fixed point; use the direction from g(x) to x to build a retraction onto the boundary, contradicting no-retraction.

validity_conditions: If g(x) != x for all x, the ray from g(x) through x meets the boundary in a well-defined point r(x), continuous in x.
r fixes the boundary (if x is already on the boundary, r(x)=x), so r is a retraction D^n -> S^{n-1}.
The no-retraction theorem forbids such r, so the assumption fails: g must have a fixed point.
proof_plan: {{AimForCont}} $\map g x \ne x$ for all $x \in \Bbb D^n$.
For each $x$, let $\map r x$ be the point where the [[Definition:Ray (Geometry)|ray]] from $\map g x$ through $x$ meets $\Bbb S^{n - 1}$.

$\map r x$ is given by solving a quadratic equation whose coefficients depend continuously on $x$, so $r$ is [[Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)|continuous]].
If $x \in \Bbb S^{n - 1}$ then $\map r x = x$.
So $r$ is a [[Definition:Retraction (Topology)|retraction]] of $\Bbb D^n$ onto $\Bbb S^{n - 1}$.
